title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection

pages.title: The pitch: a model that knows when to look things up
pages.subtitle: And that grades its own work as it writes

blocks.html: Large language models are confident liars. They generate fluent text that sounds authoritative but is frequently wrong, because they answer purely from the parameters baked in during pretraining. The obvious fix is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): before answering, fetch some documents and stuff them into the prompt. But standard RAG is clumsy in two ways the paper calls out directly.

First, it retrieves a fixed number of passages for every query, whether or not retrieval helps. Ask "Write a poem about the ocean" and RAG still drags in Wikipedia passages, diluting the prompt and sometimes derailing a task the model already does well. Second, RAG never checks whether the generated output is actually supported by the passages it retrieved. The model can cite a document and then contradict it, and nothing notices.

Self-RAG (Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation) trains a single language model to do three things on its own: decide when retrieval would help, retrieve only then, and critique both the passages and its own generations using special vocabulary words called reflection tokens. Crucially, retrieval is on demand and can fire multiple times within one answer, or never.

We introduce a new framework called Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) that improves an LLM's quality and factuality through retrieval and self-reflection. ... Self-RAG trains a single arbitrary LM that adaptively retrieves passages on-demand, and generates and reflects on retrieved passages and its own generations using special tokens, called reflection tokens.

The headline numbers: a Self-RAG (7B and 13B) trained this way outperforms ChatGPT and the retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat on open-domain QA, reasoning, and fact-verification tasks, and gives large gains in factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generation. The whole trick is teaching the model to talk to itself with a handful of new tokens.

items: Adaptive retrieval: a Retrieve token decides per-step whether to fetch passages at all.
Self-critique: ISREL, ISSUP, ISUSE tokens grade relevance, factual support, and overall usefulness.
Controllable at inference: the same trained model can be tuned soft-vs-hard on factuality without retraining.

pages.title: Why bolting retrieval onto an LLM goes wrong
pages.subtitle: Indiscriminate retrieval hurts as often as it helps

blocks.html: Imagine a smart intern who, before answering any question, sprints to the library and grabs the first three books off a shelf, even when you asked them their own opinion or asked them to write a limerick. Sometimes those books are exactly right. Sometimes they are about the wrong topic entirely, and now the intern is paraphrasing an irrelevant book instead of just answering. That is conventional RAG.
The paper frames two concrete failure modes of the standard "retrieve a fixed $k$, then generate" recipe. They matter because both are silent: nothing in the pipeline detects them.

Retrieving a fixed number of passages regardless of whether retrieval is relevant introduces irrelevant context. For tasks the model already handles from its parameters (open-ended writing, simple reasoning), this is pure noise. It dilutes the prompt and can actively lower quality. The paper notes this indiscriminate retrieval can hurt versatility and produce lower-quality outputs.

Indiscriminately retrieving and incorporating a fixed number of retrieved passages, regardless of whether retrieval is necessary or passages are relevant, diminishes LM versatility or can lead to unhelpful response generation.

blocks.text: Failure 2: outputs that ignore the evidence

blocks.html: Even when retrieval is appropriate, there is no guarantee the generation is consistent with the retrieved passages. Standard models are not explicitly trained to stay grounded, so they can confabulate facts not present in any retrieved document while still appearing to use them. The paper observes outputs are not guaranteed to be consistent with retrieved relevant passages because models are not explicitly trained to leverage and follow facts from the provided passages.

Self-RAG attacks both at once. Instead of treating retrieval as a fixed preprocessing step glued to the front of the model, it makes retrieval a decision the model makes, and makes grounding a property the model checks — both expressed in the model's own output stream.

pages.title: Reflection tokens: giving the model a vocabulary for self-doubt
pages.subtitle: Four new token families that punctuate generation

blocks.html: The core idea is almost embarrassingly simple: add new words to the model's vocabulary that don't appear in normal text, and that mean things like "I should look this up now" or "that passage was irrelevant." The model emits these reflection tokens inline, exactly the way it emits ordinary words, so a single forward pass through the same decoder both writes the answer and annotates it with self-assessment.
There are four families. One controls retrieval; three are critiques.

rows: Is my output supported by the passage?
How useful is my overall response?

blocks.html: Read that table as a checklist the model walks through. Retrieve is the gate. If it fires yes, passages come in. For each passage, ISREL says whether it's even on-topic. After generating a segment grounded in a passage, ISSUP says whether the passage actually backs up what was written (the factual-grounding check). Finally ISUSE rates the whole answer's usefulness on a 1–5 scale, independent of retrieval.

Take the prompt "How did US states get their names?" Self-RAG's output stream might look like: emit Retrieve=yes → pull passage $d_1$ → emit ISREL=relevant → write "Of the fifty states, eleven are named after individuals..." → emit ISSUP=fully supported → at the next sentence emit Retrieve=yes again for a fresh fact, grade the new passage, and so on. A different prompt like "Write a poem" would emit Retrieve=no and proceed with no retrieval at all.

Why bake these into the vocabulary instead of running a separate classifier? Because then the same autoregressive objective that learns to write also learns to critique — no extra model at inference, and the critique can condition on everything generated so far. Decoding stays a single left-to-right pass. The reflection tokens are just more tokens to predict.

pages.title: Training: distill a critic, then teach the generator
pages.subtitle: GPT-4 grades, a small critic learns to grade, the corpus gets annotated

blocks.html: We need training data where every passage and every segment is already tagged with the right reflection tokens. Hand-labeling millions of examples is hopeless. The paper's answer is a two-stage distillation: use a powerful teacher (GPT-4) to label a modest amount of data, train a small critic model $\mathcal{C}$ to reproduce those labels cheaply, then run the critic over a large corpus to produce a fully self-annotated training set for the generator $\mathcal{M}$.
GPT-4 is prompted to predict reflection tokens for sampled inputs/outputs. Those judgments are distilled into an in-house critic $\mathcal{C}$ trained by standard next-token prediction on the labels:

Term by term: $x$ is the input (the prompt, possibly with a retrieved passage), $y$ is the output segment being judged, and $r$ is the gold reflection token (e.g. ISSUP=fully supported) that GPT-4 assigned. $\mathcal{D}_{\text{critic}}$ is the dataset of these (input, output, reflection-token) triples. $p_{\mathcal{C}}(r \mid x, y)$ is the critic's predicted probability of the correct token. Maximizing the expected log-probability simply trains $\mathcal{C}$ to mimic GPT-4's grades. The paper reports the critic reaches over 90% agreement with GPT-4 predictions, so it's a faithful, cheap stand-in.

blocks.text: Stage 2 — train the generator M on critic-annotated data

blocks.html: Now run $\mathcal{C}$ offline over a large instruction-following corpus. For each example it inserts Retrieve decisions, retrieves passages where needed, and tags each segment with ISREL/ISSUP/ISUSE. The result is a corpus $\mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}}$ where reflection tokens sit inline as ordinary tokens. The generator $\mathcal{M}$ is then trained with the plain next-token objective over this augmented sequence:

Here $\mathcal{M}$ learns to predict both the real output tokens $y$ and the reflection tokens $r$ jointly, conditioned on input $x$. Because critique tokens are now just part of the target sequence, no special loss is needed — it's vanilla language-model training. The two big payoffs: (1) the generator learns to generate reflection tokens itself, so at test time it needs no separate critic; (2) the retriever is only invoked during this offline annotation, so the expensive retrieve-and-grade loop is amortized away from training-time backprop.

Notice the elegance of the split: the critic absorbs the expensive GPT-4 supervision once; the generator inherits all that judgment for free as ordinary tokens. This is the same distillation logic behind much of instruction tuning, but applied to meta-judgments about retrieval and grounding rather than to answers.

pages.title: Inference: segment-level beam search with tunable critique
pages.subtitle: Adaptive retrieval, then score candidates by their own grades

blocks.html: At inference Self-RAG generates segment by segment. At each step it first predicts a Retrieve token. Because reflection tokens are real vocabulary, the model assigns them probabilities, and that gives a clean knob for adaptive retrieval: retrieve only when the model is confident enough that retrieval helps.

blocks.text: The retrieval gate is just a threshold

blocks.html: Let the model's normalized probability of Retrieve=yes be compared against a threshold $\delta$. Retrieval is triggered when:

The numerator is the probability mass the model puts on retrieving; the denominator normalizes over the yes/no choice. $\delta$ is a single user-set knob: lower $\delta$ means retrieve more eagerly (favoring factuality), higher $\delta$ means retrieve only when very sure (favoring speed and fluency). The same trained model spans this whole trade-off with no retraining — that's the "controllable" claim.

blocks.text: When it does retrieve: parallel candidates, then rank

blocks.html: If retrieval fires, the model processes the top-$K$ passages in parallel, generating one candidate continuation per passage. Each candidate carries its own critique tokens — its ISREL, ISSUP, ISUSE grades. A segment-level beam search then keeps the best continuations, where each candidate's score combines its language-model probability with a critic score $\mathcal{S}$ built from those reflection tokens:

Each $s_t$ is the (normalized) probability the model assigns to the desirable value of critique token $t$ — for example $s_{\texttt{ISSUP}}$ is the probability of fully supported. Each $w_t$ is a tunable weight saying how much that dimension matters. Summing the weighted grades gives one scalar per candidate. The final ranking score is the LM likelihood adjusted by $\mathcal{S}$, so a fluent-but-unsupported continuation gets penalized relative to a well-grounded one.

This is the lever that makes grounding actually win at decode time. Beam search normally chases pure likelihood; here the critique tokens reshape the objective so the beam prefers segments the model itself judges relevant and supported. And because the $w_t$ are inference-time weights, a deployment that cares about citation precision can crank $w_{\texttt{ISSUP}}$ up — again, no retraining.

items: Adaptive: $\delta$ decides if retrieval happens at all, per segment.
Parallel: top-$K$ passages each spawn a graded candidate.
Controllable: weights $w_t$ reweight relevance vs. support vs. usefulness at test time.

pages.title: Beating ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2
pages.subtitle: Six tasks: QA, reasoning, fact-checking, long-form generation

blocks.html: The evaluation spans short-form QA (PopQA, TriviaQA), a fact-verification task (PubHealth), multiple-choice reasoning (ARC-Challenge), and long-form generation (a biography generation task scored by FactScore, and the ASQA long-form QA task scored by correctness and citation precision/recall). Baselines include vanilla and retrieval-augmented LLMs both with and without retrieval — among them ChatGPT, Llama2-chat (7B/13B), Alpaca, and Llama2 + standard RAG.

The central finding is stated plainly: Self-RAG significantly outperforms prior open-source LLMs and their retrieval-augmented variants, and on several tasks it beats ChatGPT too, despite being a far smaller, open model.

Self-RAG (7B and 13B) outperforms ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat on Open-domain QA, reasoning and fact verification tasks, and it shows significant gains in improving factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generations relative to these models.

rows: Highest among open models; tops ChatGPT-no-retrieval

blocks.html: The two long-form tasks are where the self-critique earns its keep. On the biography task, FactScore measures the fraction of generated facts that are actually supported — exactly what ISSUP was trained to encourage — and Self-RAG posts a large jump over standard RAG. On ASQA, citation precision and recall measure whether each claim is correctly attributed to a source, and the critique-weighted beam search drives substantial improvements. Grounding that the model checks turns into grounding the metrics can see.

Ablations confirm the parts are load-bearing: removing the critique-driven retrieval or the reflection-token scoring degrades performance, and the adaptive-retrieval threshold $\delta$ traces out a real factuality-vs-efficiency frontier — proof that the controllability knob isn't cosmetic.

pages.title: Why Self-RAG mattered
pages.subtitle: From bolt-on retrieval to retrieval as a learned behavior

blocks.html: Self-RAG's lasting contribution is conceptual: it reframes retrieval from an external pipeline stage into a behavior the model learns and controls. The model decides when to retrieve, judges what it gets back, and grades its own grounding — all in one decoder, all expressed as ordinary tokens. That collapse of "retriever + generator + verifier" into a single self-reflective LM is the idea everyone took away.

items: No more blind retrieval: the Retrieve gate skips retrieval when it would only add noise, restoring versatility on tasks the model already handles.
Grounding becomes measurable mid-generation: ISSUP turns "is this supported?" into a token the model predicts and the decoder can optimize for.
One model, many operating points: the threshold $\delta$ and critique weights $w_t$ let one trained checkpoint be tuned for factuality, citation precision, or speed without retraining.

blocks.text: Where it sits in the lineage

blocks.html: Self-RAG builds on the original RAG line of work (Lewis et al., 2020) and dense retrievers, but its self-critique machinery echoes a broader 2022–2023 wave of models grading their own outputs — the same instinct as chain-of-thought verification and self-refinement. Its distillation recipe (GPT-4 → small critic → annotated corpus) is the now-standard pattern of using a strong teacher to bootstrap supervision that would otherwise be unlabelable.

Its influence shows up wherever "agentic" or "active" retrieval is discussed: systems that decide for themselves when to call a tool, then check whether the result was useful. The reflection-token idea — special vocabulary that carries control and self-assessment signals inline — anticipated later work on tool-use tokens and self-verifying generation. Self-RAG is the paper that made "the model should decide when to look things up, and check its own homework" a concrete, trainable objective rather than a slogan.

The practical legacy is just as real: an open 7B/13B model matching or beating ChatGPT on knowledge-intensive and long-form-factuality tasks showed that how a model uses retrieval can matter more than raw scale — a hopeful message for everyone working below frontier model sizes.
